analysis.one_liner: Restores canceled Arctic Refuge oil leases and limits court review of drilling permits.
analysis.headline: Solely sponsored by Alaska's lone House Democrat with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the House Natural Resources Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced the Interior Department to reissue Arctic National Wildlife Refuge oil and gas leases that the Biden administration canceled, hold a second lease sale, and bar the President or Interior from canceling those leases in the future. It would have ratified all permits for the coastal plain drilling program as satisfying the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and other laws, withdrawn a draft environmental review and a proposed rule protecting the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, and stripped courts of the power to review the drilling approvals — except that leaseholders could still sue to force agencies to act. It died in committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil companies that bid on Arctic Refuge coastal plain tracts in the January 2021 lease sale would get their leases reissued, and future bidders would gain a mandated second lease sale with leases protected from cancellation. Alaska's oil and gas workforce and the state's energy economy would gain activity, royalties, and jobs if drilling proceeds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies bidding on Arctic Refuge tracts

how_it_helps.text: Within 30 days of enactment, Interior would have to accept the highest bids received on January 6, 2021 for six coastal plain lease tracts and reissue those leases without modification [S2].
Interior would have to conduct a second ANWR lease sale by December 22, 2024, and the President and Interior could no longer cancel issued leases unless the lessee violates lease terms [S2].

All permits, biological opinions, and approvals for the coastal plain leasing program would be deemed to satisfy the Endangered Species Act, NEPA, ANILCA, and administrative law requirements, and agencies would be directed to reinstate or maintain them [S2].

No court could review any approval for the drilling program, including lawsuits already pending, with only the D.C. Circuit hearing challenges to the provision itself; leaseholders alone could petition a court to force agency action, on a deadline of no more than 90 days [S3].

The bill would nullify the Interior Secretary's 2021 temporary halt on coastal plain leasing activities (Secretarial Order 3401) and the leasing-moratorium portions of Executive Order 13990, and bar any federal funds from carrying them out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the environmental cost of industrial development in the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain, an area used for calving caribou and subsistence hunting, and would lose the usual ability to challenge drilling permits in court. Federal oversight would be limited: the supplemental environmental review and the proposed National Petroleum Reserve protections would be withdrawn, and agencies could not issue similar rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and future court challengers

drawbacks.text: The bill would lock in drilling approvals while removing judicial review, so members of the public, conservation groups, and Alaska Native communities could not challenge the permits in court; only leaseholders get a court path, and only to speed agency action [S3].

It would override environmental laws case-by-case by declaring existing approvals sufficient under the Endangered Species Act, NEPA, and administrative procedure, and would withdraw the supplemental environmental impact statement and a proposed rule for the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska [S2].
Despite the title's reference to fisheries protection, the bill text contains no fisheries provisions; its sections address oil and gas leasing, rule withdrawal, and judicial review [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for it is Alaska's dependence on resource development: Congress directed a leasing program in the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and the bill argues Interior's cancellation of the leases exceeded the Secretary's delegated authority [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains — reissued leases, a mandated second sale, protection from cancellation — flow to a handful of oil companies and to Alaska's energy economy. The costs fall broadly: development in one of the country's most pristine wild areas, weakened environmental review, and an unusual strip of court access for everyone except the leaseholders. The bill would also have curtailed executive authority over federal lands, a constitutional question courts never got to weigh because the bill died. On balance the benefits are narrow and concentrated while the costs are diffuse and public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Peltola of Alaska introduced the bill on May 1, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S1].
No cosponsors signed on from either party [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote after the referral; the bill never advanced in committee before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the canceled ANWR leases stayed canceled and the National Petroleum Reserve rulemaking and supplemental environmental review stood; the companies that would have received reissued leases gained nothing, and the public kept existing protections for the coastal plain and its court access.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The refuge, its defenders, and the public

for.name: Mary Peltola
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it was her sole action, with no other members joining her.

against.name: Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it received no hearing, markup, or vote after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party — 0 of 224 House Republicans and 0 of 216 House Democrats — despite Republican control of the committee where it sat.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies (Arctic coastal plain lessees and bidders)
industries.note: The bill would have reissued six canceled coastal plain lease tracts to the January 2021 high bidders, mandated a second lease sale, barred future lease cancellations, and prevented anyone but the leaseholders from challenging the permits in court [S2, S3]. The industry's gain would come at the public's cost in environmental protection and court access [S3].

industries.industry: Alaska energy workforce and petroleum support services
industries.note: Resumed leasing would support exploration, construction, and drilling jobs and state revenue if development proceeds, benefits that depend on companies actually developing the tracts [S3].
